label: hv-nanopub-format
topic: How a harvested biological statement should be written as an unsigned nanopublication (assertion / provenance / pubinfo), with a template and three filled examples
summary:
Wrote one unsigned template and three filled example .trig files, but none has been parsed by an RDF parser (rdflib is not installed), and the harvest is short of the 8-12 asked for. The only check on the files was a count of four graph blocks each and a search confirming no ORCID.

**What was harvested.** Four format rules from the nanopub guidelines and three base-count statements, seven in total. No Kleiber, Hardy-Weinberg or other laws were harvested, because I did not open a primary source for them in the time available.

**Validation 1: Chargaff's second parity rule (one strand has A about equal to T and G about equal to C).** I fetched three genomes from NCBI and counted bases. The 5% tolerance is my own choice, not from a source.

| Genome | Accession | A/T | G/C | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Phage lambda | NC_001416.1 | 1.029 | 1.128 | Fail (A/T passes, G/C does not) |
| Phage phiX174 | NC_001422.1 | 0.767 | 1.084 | Fail (single-stranded virion, so out of the rule's scope) |
| Human mitochondrion | NC_012920.1 | 1.252 | 0.419 | Fail |

These are three small genomes; they say nothing about large chromosomes.

**Validation 2: format rules against the existing drafts.** The 10 files in `holdout/nanopubs/unsigned` each have the four named graphs and no ORCID line: pass. The 21 files in `math-bio-theorems/nanopubs/unsigned` did not match my graph-name pattern and each has 2 ORCID lines. I did not open them, so whether that is a real problem or just different graph naming is unknown.

**Registry check.** Grep for "chargaff" or "parity rule" in `lean`, `tracks/lean` and `tracks/research` returned no files, so the rule is not in the law registry or research track.

**Known gaps in the files.**
- The template is example 1 with the claim id, slug and accession swapped for placeholders; it still carries the lambda numbers and label.
- `delphi:formalStatement`, `delphi:Hypothesis` and `delphi:Evidence` are my guesses at ontology terms; I did not check them against the Delphi ontology.
- `dct:created` is date-only precision (midnight placeholder).
- The claim's primary paper (Rudner, Karkas and Chargaff, 1968) was not opened, so the .trig files cite only the NCBI records.

The repo was not edited; nothing was signed, published or sent.

Files are in D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents4/hv-nanopub-format:
- template-unsigned.trig
- example-1-lambda.trig
- example-2-phix174.trig
- example-3-human-mito.trig
- gen.sh

findings.claim: Format rule: a nanopublication head contains exactly one typing quad and one link each to assertion, provenance and publication info. Formal: |{q in H : q = (N, rdf:type, np:Nanopublication)}| = 1, likewise for np:hasAssertion, np:hasProvenance, np:hasPublicationInfo. Falsifying test: count those four predicates in the Head graph of every draft; any count != 1 fails.
findings.evidence_quote: There is exactly one quad of the form '[N] rdf:type np:Nanopublication [H]'.
findings.value: The 10 drafts in holdout/nanopubs/unsigned each show the 4 named graphs (grep count only): pass. The 21 math-bio-theorems drafts did not match my grep pattern: not assessed.
findings.confidence: high for the rule (page opened via WebFetch summary); medium for the check (regex, not an RDF parser)

findings.claim: Format rule: the provenance graph must refer to the assertion graph. Formal: exists a triple in P whose subject or object is the assertion IRI A. Test: parse each draft and check P mentions A.
findings.evidence_quote: Triples in [P] have at least one reference to [A].
findings.value: My four files each have 'sub:assertion prov:wasAttributedTo ...' in sub:provenance (by construction, not parser-checked).

findings.claim: Format rule: the publication-info graph must refer to the nanopublication IRI; attribution and timestamp are SHOULD, not MUST. Formal: exists a triple in I mentioning N. Test: parse and check; also flag drafts lacking dct:created or dct:creator.
findings.evidence_quote: MUST be the nanopublication URI and SHOULD contain attribution and timestamp
findings.value: My files carry dct:created and dct:creator (a software agent, no human ORCID).
findings.confidence: high for the rule; the quote is as relayed by the fetch tool's summary

findings.claim: Format rule: trusty URIs are recommended, not part of well-formedness, so an unsigned draft with a temp URI is still a well-formed nanopublication.
findings.evidence_quote: are the recommended way of assigning integrity keys to nanopublications
findings.value: All four files use http://purl.org/nanopub/temp/... URIs, with no hash and no signature.
findings.confidence: medium (quote is a fragment relayed by the fetch summary)

findings.claim: Chargaff's second parity rule on phage lambda. Formal: on the deposited strand, |nA/nT - 1| <= 0.05 and |nG/nC - 1| <= 0.05 (assumptions: double-stranded genome; the 0.05 tolerance is mine). Prediction: both ratios within 5% of 1. Measured: A 12334, C 11362, G 12820, T 11986; A/T = 1.029, G/C = 1.128. FAIL (A/T passes, G/C does not). Not in the repo: grep for 'chargaff|parity rule' in lean, tracks/lean, tracks/research returned no files. Open dataset: NCBI RefSeq genomes; test: per-genome single-strand base counts against the tolerance.
findings.evidence_quote: NC_001416.1 Enterobacteria phage lambda, complete genome
findings.confidence: high for the counts; the tolerance is an arbitrary choice

findings.claim: Chargaff's second parity rule on phage phiX174. Same formal statement. Prediction: both ratios within 5% of 1. Measured: A 1291, C 1157, G 1254, T 1684; A/T = 0.767, G/C = 1.084. FAIL on both. The virion DNA is single-stranded, so the rule's double-strand assumption is not met; recorded as out of scope rather than a refutation.
findings.evidence_quote: NC_001422.1 Escherichia phage phiX174, complete genome
findings.confidence: high for the counts; the single-stranded scope note is from my own knowledge, not a source opened in this run

findings.claim: Chargaff's second parity rule on the human mitochondrial genome. Same formal statement. Prediction: both ratios within 5% of 1. Measured: A 5124, C 5181, G 2169, T 4094, plus one N excluded; A/T = 1.252, G/C = 0.419. FAIL on both. Says nothing about nuclear chromosomes.
findings.evidence_quote: NC_012920.1 Homo sapiens mitochondrion, complete genome

findings.claim: Existing drafts: the 21 files under math-bio-theorems/nanopubs/unsigned each contain 2 lines matching 'orcid.org/0' and none of my four graph-name patterns; the 10 holdout drafts contain 4 graph blocks and 0 ORCID lines.
findings.value: 21 files: 0 graph-pattern matches, 2 ORCID lines each. 10 files: 4 graph blocks, 0 ORCID lines.
findings.confidence: low on what it means: I did not open any math-bio-theorems draft, so the ORCID lines could be legitimate citations and the graphs may simply be named differently

key_claims: Four unsigned .trig files were written (one template, three examples); none was parsed by an RDF parser.
Chargaff's second parity rule fails a 5% tolerance on all three small genomes tested; phiX174 is out of the rule's scope because it is single-stranded.
The 10 holdout drafts match the four-graph structure and carry no ORCID; the 21 math-bio-theorems drafts were not assessed beyond a grep.
Chargaff's rule is not in lean, tracks/lean or tracks/research.
Only 7 statements were harvested, not the 8-12 asked for.
lay_summary: A nanopublication is a tiny digital note with three parts: what is claimed, where it came from, and who wrote the note and when.
I wrote a blank form for such notes and filled it in three times, without signing or publishing anything.
To have something real to write down, I tested an old rule that says one strand of DNA has about as many A letters as T letters, and as many G as C.
I counted the letters in three small genomes and the rule did not hold within 5 percent in any of them, which is a useful thing to record honestly.
My files have not yet been checked by a proper reading program, so they might still contain typing mistakes.

glossary.nanopublication: A very small machine-readable record of one claim, with its source and its author information attached.
glossary.assertion: The part of the record that states the claim itself.
glossary.provenance: The part that says where the claim came from and how it was made.
glossary.pubinfo: The part that says who made the record, when, and under what licence.
glossary.head: The part that ties the other three parts together into one record.
glossary.TriG / .trig: A text file format for writing linked data split into named groups.
glossary.RDF: A standard way to write facts as subject-verb-object triples that computers can read.
glossary.quad: A triple plus the name of the group (graph) it belongs to.
glossary.graph: A named group of triples inside the file.
glossary.IRI / URI: A web-style address used as a unique name for a thing.
glossary.trusty URI: An address that includes a fingerprint of the content, so changes can be detected.
glossary.unsigned: Not stamped with anyone's digital key, so nobody has vouched for it.
glossary.ORCID: A personal ID number for researchers.
glossary.software agent: A program, not a person, named as the maker of a record.
glossary.Chargaff's second parity rule: The observation that within a single DNA strand, A and T counts are roughly equal, and G and C counts are roughly equal.
glossary.genome: The full DNA sequence of an organism or virus.
glossary.mitochondrion: A small part of a cell with its own short DNA.
glossary.single-stranded: DNA made of one strand instead of the usual paired two.
glossary.tolerance: How far a measured number may be from the predicted one and still count as a pass.
glossary.accession: The catalogue number of a sequence in a public database.
glossary.FASTA: A plain text format for DNA sequences.
glossary.RefSeq: NCBI's curated collection of reference sequences.
glossary.grep: A tool that searches text for a pattern.
glossary.Lean: A program that checks mathematical proofs.
glossary.ontology: An agreed list of terms and how they relate.

could_not_find: RDF parser validation of the four .trig files: rdflib is not installed, so syntax is unverified.
The primary paper for Chargaff's second parity rule (Rudner, Karkas and Chargaff, 1968, PNAS): not opened, DOI not confirmed, so not cited in the files.
Whether delphi:formalStatement, delphi:Hypothesis and delphi:Evidence exist in the Delphi ontology: not checked.
The content of the 21 math-bio-theorems drafts: only grep counts were taken, none was read.
Harvest items 8-12: only 7 statements were harvested; no Kleiber, Hardy-Weinberg or other laws, because no primary source was opened for them.
The nanopub guideline quotes come through the fetch tool's summary, not the raw page; the wording should be rechecked against the page.
recommendations: Parse the four .trig files with a real RDF parser (the np jar or rdflib) before anyone builds on them.
Strip the lambda-specific numbers and label out of template-unsigned.trig and replace them with placeholders.
Check the three delphi: terms I guessed against the ontology, or swap them for the terms the holdout drafts already use.
Open one math-bio-theorems draft to see whether its two ORCID lines are a signer identity or a citation, and how its graphs are named.
If Chargaff's rule is wanted as a law, test it on large bacterial chromosomes, where it is usually claimed to hold, with the tolerance fixed in advance.
